transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-10
Start time: 14:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Location: Zoom / internal enablement room
Attendees: Maya Patel (AE), Carlos Nguyen (SE), Eli Zhang (SWE), Alex Kim (Enablement), Priya Rao (role-play), Tom Gallagher (role-play), Li Wei (role-play)

Agenda: 1) Quick 5-min framing, 2) 25-min live demo (role-play), 3) 20-min objection handling + positioning, 4) Recap + next steps

[00:00] Alex (Enablement): Okay, good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. We're doing a mock pitch targeted to an Acera Financial buyer persona, aim is to tighten the reg/compliance story and get crisp answers on deployment options. Maya, you want to set the scene?

[00:20] Maya (AE): Yep, thanks Alex. Quick context: Acera is a mid-size payments platform, heavy on PCI-ish controls, they care about auditability, key management, and they have a platform team that dislikes persistent internet egress. Priya and Tom are role-playing head of AI and CTO. Goal is to convince them Redwood can run in their environment with predictable latency and transparent cost, and to move them to a pilot.

[00:45] Priya (Role-play): Hi, thanks—just to be clear, our main concern is data leaving our VPC, and we need attestation that logs are tamper-proof. Also want a performance SLO for token latency under realistic load.

[01:10] Carlos (SE): Totally, that maps to what we've seen. We'll show both the private deployment and dedicated options; the private option keeps control-plane in your VPC, offers KMS/HSM integration, full audit logs, and on-prem option if needed. For latency, Dedicated gives the most predictable p99s with reserved GPU pools, while Hosted gives faster time-to-value.

[01:40] Tom (Role-play): Okay, but cost is a real constraint. How do we balance dedicated infra expense vs hosted per-token costs?

[01:55] Eli (SWE): Maybe quick plug: Redwood Optimize suggests batching and quantization profiles tied to workload which can materially change unit economics. We can run an analysis off sample traffic to recommend a configuration.

[02:15] [Demo start]
[02:15] Carlos (SE): Alright, I'm sharing screen. First slide — short architecture. (mumble) Note: the diagram shows smart routing — requests can be routed to Dedicated or fallback to Hosted variants during peaks. That allows a predictable base capacity and burst cost control.

[03:10] Priya (Role-play): Can you show an example of key management? We need to know where keys live.

[03:25] Carlos (SE): Sure. Here in the console — under Security -> Keys — you can see KMS bindings. For Private deployments we integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM, keys never leave your HSM. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption but you can also bring your own key in many cases. (slight pause) Note: transcript messed up this part a bit — I said 'envelope' and the recording picked up 'invelope' earlier.

[04:05] [04:05] Priya (Role-play): Audit logs — what granularity are you capturing? We need to show sequence of events for compliance audits.

[04:20] Carlos (SE): We capture per-request metadata, model/version, prompt hash (optional), requester token id, and routing decision. Logs are tamper-evident when shipped through your logging endpoint; for Private installs we can support signed append-only logs. There's a small caveat: some open models include user-provided data in cache snapshots so we recommend metadata-only retention by default.

[05:00] Tom (Role-play): How about data residency? Europe vs US?

[05:10] Maya (AE): We have region pins for both Hosted and Dedicated. Private obviously runs in your region/VPC. For enterprise we map the control plane locality and storage locality as part of the contract.

[05:30] [06:00] Carlos (SE): Demoing a request flow now — small script that simulates 150 concurrent users, 50 tokens per request. Notice the batching behavior: Redwood runtime groups similar sequence lengths and uses continuous batching to improve throughput. On Dedicated you can tune batch windows to hit latency SLOs.

[06:45] Priya (Role-play): What's the p99 for small seq (<=128) on a Dedicated T4-like profile?

[06:55] Carlos (SE): In our benchmarks on xG P4-ish hardware we typically see p50 ~40ms, p95 ~85ms, p99 ~150-180ms depending on model and KV cache. We should avoid quoting exact numbers without a pilot benchmark — there's variability by model. (FYI sometimes we talk 'P4' but customers call everything 'GPU' so adjust language.)

[07:30] Alex (Enablement): Quick note for Maya — when Priya asks about numbers, don't give absolute claims, offer to run a pilot to provide customer-specific SLAs.

[07:50] Maya (AE): Good call. Okay Carlos, let's show a stall scenario — what happens if Dedicated runs out of capacity?

[08:05] Carlos (SE): Smart routing kicks in: policy-based fallback to a compatible Hosted variant or a lower-precision quantized model. That lets apps stay online with graceful degradation. We also support canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies configured at route level.

[08:35] Priya (Role-play): What about model hallucinations — does Redwood help with evaluation and continuous quality monitoring?

[08:50] Eli (SWE): Yes, Redwood Optimize ties quality monitoring to prompt sets and can trigger regression alerts if output distribution shifts. You can attach golden prompt sets and get diffs on tokens, helpful for regulated checks.

[09:20] [09:20] Priya (Role-play): I want to see the SAML/SSO and RBAC workflows — we can't have broad access to production keys.

[09:35] Carlos (SE): In the console we integrate with SAML SSO, role-based access, and per-token scoping. We can show how to lock the KMS key to a narrower set of roles; you combine that with audit logs for full traceability. (audio: slight overlap, 'K-M-S' was said slowly and got turned into letters in the transcript)

[10:10] [10:10] Demo clip ends (we recorded a short walkthrough)

[10:25] Tom (Role-play): Alright, now push me on pricing. Our procurement hates per-token surprises. How do we make costs predictable?

[10:40] Maya (AE): Good question. We typically recommend Reserved capacity (Dedicated) with monthly commitments for predictable unit economics, plus Optimize to tune batching and quantization. For spike protection you can add burst credits or fallback rules. We'll also provide an estimated bill run using your sample traces for the pilot.

[11:10] Priya (Role-play): And if we choose Hosted for initial testing, do we get any contractual guarantees?

[11:22] Maya (AE): Hosted is first-party SLA for availability, but for latency guarantees we usually move into Dedicated/Committed contracts. We can include an SLO addendum for pilots if needed.

[11:40] [11:40] Objection handling practice — pricing angle.

[11:45] Alex (Enablement): Role-play exercise: Tom will start with a hard 'we can build this ourselves cheaper' objection. Maya, take first rebuttal, Carlos jump in with technical proof points.

[12:00] Tom (Role-play): We could probably stitch together open-source models on our infra, run a small cluster, and save a lot of money.

[12:10] Maya (AE): Sure, you could, but building inference reliably at scale is a hidden cost. Our customers cite ops time, kernel perf, and the cost of rolling your own fallback and canary systems as the main drivers. Also, we provide features like per-route tracing and regression alerts out of the box.

[12:35] Carlos (SE): Technical point — maintaining optimized kernels across model versions and sequence lengths is non-trivial. Redwood's runtime picks kernels based on architecture and CPU/GPU characteristics; we handle the compiler/kernel mapping so your platform team doesn't need to chase perf regressions. That reduces engineering debt.

[13:00] Priya (Role-play): Okay but give me an example where Redwood saved cost vs naive self-hosting.

[13:10] Eli (SWE): We had a customer who moved from naive batching to our continuous batching + prefix caching and saw token cost drop by ~30% for chat-like workloads. (numbers are illustrative; always tie to a pilot)

[13:35] Tom (Role-play): I want to push on security certifications — SOC2 is table stakes, but any ISO, FedRamp?

[13:45] Carlos (SE): We are SOC2 Type II; for other certifications we often work with customers to map controls in Private or Dedicated deployments. For FedRAMP or ISO, scope is typically part of a larger enterprise conversation and may involve our compliance team. Offer to get the security pack.

[14:10] [14:10] Role-play escalation — Tom asks a tough question on incident response.

[14:15] Maya (AE): If there's an incident we have runbooks for failover and rollback; for Dedicated we can do cross-region failover and for Private we hand over those runbooks and can provide training. We also provide tracing hooks so you can debug request paths.

[14:40] Priya (Role-play): I'm worried about KV cache and PII leakage. If the model caches prefixes, can sensitive tokens leak?

[14:55] Carlos (SE): By default KV cache is ephemeral and not persisted to long-term storage. For regulated environments we disable caching of raw user input and only cache model-side keys; we can also configure prompt redaction pipelines before caching.

[15:20] Alex (Enablement): Note here, when you talk about cache, keep it simple: say 'we can disable persistence and run redaction pipelines' — avoid going deep into 'kv' jargon unless the technical buyer asks.

[15:40] [15:40] Pricing counter-rebuttal practice — Maya tries a different angle.

[15:45] Maya (AE): If you have existing infra, great. The question is: do you want to invest team cycles and calendar-time to reach production parity? Redwood buys you time and instrumentation to iterate faster. For procurement, we often propose a small pilot with clear exit criteria.

[16:10] Tom (Role-play): Pilot duration? We prefer short engagements.

[16:20] Maya (AE): Typically 4–6 weeks. Enough to run benchmarks and integrate basic telemetry, and provide a bill estimate.

[16:40] [17:00] Quick coaching break — Alex pauses the role-play and gives feedback on tone and message rhythm.

[17:05] Alex (Enablement): Two tangible coaching points: 1) when you bring up audits, cite the exact artifacts we can deliver (SOC2 report, audit log schema, KMS integration steps), 2) avoid over-quantifying perf without data — instead, promise a pilot benchmark.

[17:30] Maya (AE): Good. Carlos, any suggestions to make the demo flow tighter?

[17:40] Carlos (SE): Yes — start with the ask: 'we will demo how we keep keys in your HSM, how audit logs look, and how we fail gracefully under capacity pressure' — then do three quick demos in sequence: KMS binding, audit log playback, fallback routing. Keep each to 2 minutes.

[18:05] [18:05] We replayed the shorter KMS clip (we're recording snippets for enablement)

[18:40] Priya (Role-play): The KMS demo was clear but I want to see the actual policy statement.

[18:55] Carlos (SE): We'll attach a sample policy in the follow-up. (note in the recording I mispronounced 'policy' as 'polessi' once)

[19:10] [19:10] Objection library practice — we go through 3 common objections: build vs buy, latency, and certifications.

[19:15] Maya (AE): For build vs buy — short value props: reduce time-to-prod, reduce ops headcount needed to stay current on model kernels, provide observability and rollout tools.

[19:45] Tom (Role-play): Latency is king for us — especially on fraud decisions where 200ms can be too slow.

[19:55] Carlos (SE): Acknowledged. For fraud decisions we usually recommend a two-tier approach: small, highly-optimized local models for real-time decisions and Redwood for secondary scoring or complex reasoning. Or use a low-latency Dedicated tier with strict batch windows.

[20:25] Priya (Role-play): Last question: what does a successful pilot look like to you?

[20:35] Maya (AE): Agreed success criteria: 1) integrate Redwood SDKs into one service path, 2) run a performance benchmark with your sample traffic and meet agreed p95 SLO, 3) validate audit logs and KMS integration, 4) cost estimate within acceptable % of your runway.

[21:00] [21:00] Final practice — Maya closes the pitch with a compact 90-second summary.

[21:05] Maya (AE): Thanks Priya/Tom. If we summarize quickly: Redwood gives you a unified runtime across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private; we can run in your VPC and integrate with KMS/HSM; Optimize helps cut unit cost with batching and quantization; and we back rollouts with tracing and fallback policies so you don't go dark during peaks. Proposed next step: 4–6 week pilot, we run benchmark and deliver a bill estimate. Any final questions?

[21:45] Priya (Role-play): No, that covers it. My only ask is that the follow-up includes exact docs for KMS and the audit schema.

[22:00] [22:00] Recap + feedback loop: Alex collects feedback: pacing, technical depth, objection phrasing.

[22:10] Alex (Enablement): Quick notes: Maya — tighten the opening pitch to 30 seconds; Carlos — have a 90s script for the KMS demo; Eli — capture the example numbers we used in a 'benchmarks are illustrative' footnote.

[23:00] [23:00] Closing — agree next steps and owners (see action items).

[23:10] Carlos (SE): I'll record the SOC2/KMS snippet and make a trimmed version for the playbook.

[23:20] Maya (AE): I'll draft the tailored deck and send to the group for vetting before we push to the enablement repo.

[23:35] Tom (Role-play): Thanks team — tough but useful practice.

[23:50] End of recording. Remaining time used for quick notes and scheduling follow-up.

Notes on transcription quality: medium. There are a few mis-heard technical terms (e.g., "invelope" vs "envelope", "polessi" vs "policy") and occasional speaker attribution drift during overlapping talk. The timestamps are approximate and were inserted every ~30-90 seconds during the call.

Referenced artifacts: short demo clips (KMS, audit logs, fallback routing), Regulated Vertical playbook slide deck, sample benchmark spreadsheet (to be attached in follow-up), enablement scenario repo link (internal).

End of transcript.
